title: PLACE ATTACHMENT: CONCEPTUAL AND EMPIRICAL QUESTIONS

findings.antecedent: Place attachment scale (overall)
findings.quote: As a result we obtained a Cronbach's alpha of 0.85 for the scale as a whole, indicating a high degree of reliability.

findings.antecedent: Place attachment subscales (house, neighbourhood, city)
findings.quote: obtaining an alpha of 0.70 for the three cases.

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house, neighbourhood, city)
findings.mechanism: Different spatial scales evoke different levels of affective bonds.
findings.quote: An analysis of variance between the three scores revealed the existence of significant differences between the three ranges (F(2,350) = 3·69; p<0.001).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (neighbourhood vs house)
findings.mechanism: Neighbourhoods may have less personal significance or fewer strong affective bonds compared to one's house.
findings.quote: global attachment to neighbourhood is significantly less than global attachment to house (F(1,175) = 5·15; p<0.05)

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (neighbourhood vs city)
findings.mechanism: Neighbourhoods may have less personal significance or fewer strong affective bonds compared to the broader city.
findings.quote: global attachment to neighbourhood... less than... to city (F(1,175) = 5.91; p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house vs city)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to one's house and city are comparable in strength.
findings.quote: there are no significant differences between house and city attachment.

findings.antecedent: Sex (women vs men)
findings.consequent: Global place attachment scores (house, neighbourhood, city)
findings.mechanism: Sociocultural factors or gender roles may influence the development of affective bonds to places.
findings.quote: main effect of sex (F(1,158) = 4·41; p = 0.037) suggesting that women develop more attachment to the house... neighbourhood... and the city than men

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house, neighbourhood, city) * Age group (younger, intermediate, older)
findings.mechanism: The salience of different spatial scales for forming affective bonds changes across the lifespan.
findings.quote: a significant interaction between spatial range and age was found (F(4,314) = 2.53; p = 0.04).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house, neighbourhood, city) for older adults (age 3)
findings.mechanism: For older adults, affective bonds are equally strong across house, neighbourhood, and city.
findings.quote: no differences in the older group regarding attachment level to house, neighbourhood, and city (F(2,172) = 0.056; p = 0.946).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house, neighbourhood, city) for younger adults (age 1)
findings.mechanism: Younger adults show varying affective bonds across different spatial scales.
findings.quote: differences in these parameters in the younger (age = 1) (F(2,172) = 3-17; p=0.044)

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (city vs house/neighbourhood) for younger adults (age 1)
findings.mechanism: Younger adults may have stronger affective bonds to the broader city, possibly due to exploration or social opportunities.
findings.quote: attachment to city was significantly higher (F(1,173) = 6-14; p = 0.014) than house and neighbourhood attachment.

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house vs neighbourhood) for younger adults (age 1)
findings.mechanism: For younger adults, affective bonds to house and neighbourhood are comparable.
findings.quote: no differences were found between these two spatial ranges (F(1,173) = 0.24; p=0.625).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house, neighbourhood, city) for intermediate adults (age 2)
findings.mechanism: Intermediate adults show varying affective bonds across different spatial scales.
findings.quote: intermediate age groups (age = 2) (F(2,172) =6.39; p=0.002).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range of attachment (house vs neighbourhood) for intermediate adults (age 2)
findings.mechanism: Intermediate adults may have stronger affective bonds to their house, possibly due to family life or stability, compared to the neighbourhood.
findings.quote: higher scores in house attachment, while their attachment to the neighbourhood was the lowest (F(1,173) = 12·81; p=0.000).

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs intermediate)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the house strengthen with age.

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs intermediate)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the neighbourhood strengthen with age.
findings.quote: neighbourhood (F(1,173) = 10.08; p=0.002)

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs intermediate)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the city strengthen with age.

findings.antecedent: Age group (intermediate vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the neighbourhood continue to strengthen into older age.
findings.quote: Significant differences were also found between age groups 2 and 3 in attachment to neigh-bourhood (F(1,173) = 4.48; p=0.036)

findings.antecedent: Age group (intermediate vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the house do not significantly change between intermediate and older age.
findings.quote: no differences were noted regarding attachment to house (F(1,173 = 0.09; p=0.759)

findings.antecedent: Age group (intermediate vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the city do not significantly change between intermediate and older age.

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the house strengthen significantly from younger to older age.
findings.quote: Comparisons between age groups 1 and 3 yielded significance for house attachment (F(1,173) = 23-93; p=0.000)

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the neighbourhood strengthen significantly from younger to older age.
findings.quote: neighbourhood (F(1,173) = 25-44; p=0.000)

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger vs older)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds to the city strengthen significantly from younger to older age.

findings.antecedent: Spatial range (house, neighbourhood, city) * Attachment dimension (physical, social)
findings.mechanism: The relative importance of physical vs. social aspects of place attachment varies across different spatial scales.
findings.quote: The results revealed the existence of an interaction between both variables (F(2,352) = 17·18; p<0.0001).

findings.antecedent: Spatial range (house vs city) for social attachment
findings.mechanism: Social bonds are stronger within the intimate setting of the house compared to the broader city.
findings.quote: house attachment was greater than city attachment in the social dimension, (F(1,176) = 12.94; p<0001)

findings.antecedent: Spatial range (city vs house) for physical attachment
findings.mechanism: Physical features of the broader city may evoke stronger affective bonds than those of the house.
findings.quote: this pattern is reversed for the physical dimension, with city attachment being more impor-tant than house attachment (F(1,176) = 4.16; p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Attachment dimension (social vs physical)
findings.mechanism: Affective bonds are primarily driven by social connections rather than purely physical aspects of places.
findings.quote: a main effect was found for the dimension variable (F(1,176) = 28·99; p<0001), such that, globally, social attachment is stronger than physical attachment.

findings.antecedent: Spatial range (house, neighbourhood, city)
findings.consequent: Place attachment scores (physical and social dimensions)
findings.mechanism: When considering both physical and social dimensions, the overall strength of attachment does not differ significantly across spatial ranges.
findings.quote: no main effect regarding range attachment (house, neighbourhood, city) was found.

findings.antecedent: Social class
findings.consequent: Place attachment scores (physical and social dimensions)
findings.mechanism: Social class does not significantly influence the strength of affective bonds to places.
findings.quote: social class was eliminated from this analysis because it yielded a lack of significance.

findings.antecedent: Age group (younger, intermediate, older) * Attachment dimension (physical, social)
findings.mechanism: The relative importance of physical vs. social aspects of place attachment varies across different age groups.
findings.quote: A significant interaction was found... between age and dimension on the other.

findings.antecedent: Attachment dimension (social vs physical) for older adults (age 3)
findings.mechanism: For older adults, social and physical aspects contribute equally to place attachment.
findings.quote: no differences in the older group (F(1,174) = 1.51; p=0.220).

findings.antecedent: Attachment dimension (social vs physical) for intermediate adults (age 2)
findings.mechanism: For intermediate adults, social connections are a stronger driver of place attachment than physical aspects.
findings.quote: social attachment is greater than physical attachment in the intermediate (F(1,174) = 28-42; p =0.000).

findings.antecedent: Attachment dimension (social vs physical) for younger adults (age 1)
findings.mechanism: For younger adults, social connections are a stronger driver of place attachment than physical aspects.
findings.quote: social attachment is greater than physical attachment in the young age groups (F(1,174) = 26-34).

Mean scores in the different ranges and dimensions of attachment

limitations: The study was conducted in a medium-sized city, which might influence the significance of neighbourhood life and attachment. Results may not generalize to larger cities where distances are greater and neighbourhood activities might assume more importance.
